Diabetes insipidus and SIADH: 4

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A patient with diabetes insipidus cannot obtain enough water and develops hypernatremia. Which fluid-balance problem best explains the rising sodium when the kidneys continue producing large volumes of inappropriately dilute urine?

  1. Arginine vasopressin resistance
  2. SIADH
  3. Osmotic diuresis
  4. Free-water loss
  5. Arginine vasopressin deficiency
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Free-water loss

Inadequate antidiuresis produces dilute polyuria and can cause hypernatremia if water intake does not keep pace.

Understanding the options

Free-water loss
Inadequate antidiuresis produces dilute polyuria and can cause hypernatremia if water intake does not keep pace.
Arginine vasopressin deficiency
Central diabetes insipidus results from inadequate vasopressin secretion and can respond to desmopressin. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Arginine vasopressin resistance
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus reflects reduced renal response to vasopressin. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
SIADH
Hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine can suggest SIADH after excluding relevant alternatives. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Osmotic diuresis
Glucosuria or another poorly reabsorbed solute can cause polyuria without primary vasopressin deficiency. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
